name: Format / purpose
controls: What kind of motion piece this is and the job it has to do: the deliverable type, its typical length, aspect ratio, placement and the audience's viewing context. Format sets the constraints every other dimension works inside.
question: What kind of video is this, and what job does it do?
notes: Formats overlap constantly and industry naming is loose. A 'launch film' is often also a 'brand film'; a 'teaser' and a 'trailer' are used interchangeably by marketing teams; 'sting', 'ident' and 'bumper' mean slightly different things in broadcast vs digital. Pick one primary format (the job) and at most one secondary (the vehicle), e.g. product launch film + social ad cutdown, or explainer + kinetic typography. Length, aspect ratio and sound-off viewing are part of the format decision: social formats assume muted autoplay and 9:16 or 4:5; web heroes assume silent looping; broadcast assumes safe areas and exact durations (5, 10, 15, 30 s). Terms marked informal in `vs` are practitioner shorthand rather than standardized categories.

options.what: A 30-120 s hero film that announces a new product or major version and frames why it matters.
options.looks: High production value; product UI or hardware shown large and art-directed; bold headline cards; brand color and type locked tight; ends on logo + date or CTA.
options.motion: Choreographed camera moves over UI or renders, confident easing, beat-cut scene changes, a clear build to a hero reveal near the end.
options.use: Keynotes, launch-day homepages, Product Hunt, X/LinkedIn launch posts, press kits.
options.conveys: Ambition and arrival; 'this is a big moment'.
options.vs: A feature reveal covers one capability; a launch film sells the whole product or release. A brand film sells the company's values and may show no product at all.
options.prompt: Build a 45-75 s product launch film in 5-7 scenes: cold-open hook (0-5 s), problem or context line, 3-4 feature beats each built around one large UI or product moment with a 2-5 word headline, a hero reveal of the product name, then logo lockup with date or CTA held >= 2 s. Keep one consistent camera grammar and one accent color throughout.

options.what: A short piece that introduces a single new capability and its payoff.
options.looks: One UI surface, cropped tight on the new control; a headline naming the feature; supporting benefit line; product name small.
options.motion: Push-in to the relevant region, the feature activates once in a clean demonstration, result state held.
options.use: Release announcements, social posts, changelog embeds, in-app 'what's new' modals.
options.conveys: Momentum and focus: the product keeps getting better.
options.vs: A feature walkthrough teaches the steps to use it; a reveal only shows that it exists and why it's good.
options.prompt: Make a 10-25 s feature reveal: open on the feature name as a headline (1.5-2 s), cut or push into the one UI region that changes, demonstrate the feature once from trigger to result, hold the result >= 1.5 s, close on product name + 'Now available'. Show only one feature; crop away everything unrelated.

options.what: A step-by-step visual tour of how a feature is used, in the order a user would do it.
options.looks: Full or simplified UI screens, cursor or tap indicators, numbered step labels or callouts, consistent framing between steps.
options.motion: Cursor-led: move, click, UI responds; camera pans or zooms to follow the active region; steps separated by short holds.
options.use: Help centers, onboarding emails, sales enablement, docs pages.
options.conveys: Ease and learnability; 'you can do this in three steps'.
options.vs: A tutorial teaches a skill and may cover several features with explanation; a walkthrough stays on one feature's path. A product demo sells; a walkthrough instructs.
options.prompt: Structure as 3-6 numbered steps. For each: a short step label (e.g. '1  Select a range'), the cursor moves to the control, a click ripple, the UI responds, hold 1-1.5 s on the result before the camera moves to the next region. Keep the UI frame fixed; move the camera, not the interface.

options.what: A persuasive demonstration of the product doing real work, end to end.
options.looks: Realistic or lightly simplified UI with plausible data; real workflow from input to outcome; benefit headlines between segments.
options.motion: Realistic interaction timing slightly accelerated; zooms to the detail that matters; speed ramps over repetitive steps.
options.use: Homepages, sales decks, trade shows, paid ads.
options.conveys: Proof: the product actually does what it claims.
options.vs: A UI showcase is about how the interface looks; a demo is about what it does. A walkthrough is instructional; a demo is persuasive.
options.prompt: Show one realistic job done end to end with plausible data (real names, numbers, dates; no lorem ipsum). Compress repetitive steps with speed ramps or jump cuts; slow down and zoom 1.5-2.5x on the moment of value. Insert a 3-6 word benefit headline between each of 3-5 segments.

options.what: A piece that displays interface design itself as the subject: screens, components and states shown for their craft.
options.looks: Screens floating on a neutral or gradient ground, often tilted in 3D, multiple devices or panels arranged in grids or stacks.
options.motion: Slow orbit or tilt-shift camera drift, screens sliding past, state changes and micro-interactions looping.
options.use: Portfolio reels, Dribbble/Behance, design-system launches, agency case studies.
options.conveys: Craft and polish; visual quality of the product.
options.vs: A product demo proves function; a UI showcase admires form. Often informal: 'UI reel' in agency speak.
options.prompt: Arrange 3-8 screens or components on a calm ground (solid or subtle gradient), some tilted 10-25 degrees in perspective. Drive a slow continuous camera drift (no hard stops) and let each screen play one micro-interaction or state change in turn, staggered 300-600 ms apart.

options.what: In-product or first-run motion that orients new users to the product's core idea in seconds.
options.looks: Simplified or illustrated UI, one concept per panel, short captions, pagination dots; very light, often loopable.
options.motion: Gentle, quick, forgiving: 300-600 ms transitions, soft springs, each panel loops one idea.
options.use: App first-run carousels, empty states, welcome modals, setup flows.
options.conveys: Welcome and reassurance; low cognitive load.
options.vs: A tutorial teaches a task in depth; onboarding sets expectations and teaches the core mental model only.
options.prompt: Design 3-4 short panels (3-5 s each), each communicating one idea with a simplified UI or illustration and one line of copy <= 8 words. Transitions 300-500 ms with soft ease-out; each panel's internal animation should loop seamlessly so it works if the user lingers.

options.what: An instructional piece that teaches a viewer to accomplish a task, with explanation at each step.
options.looks: Real UI with callouts, highlight boxes, zoom insets, captions or voiceover text; chapter markers for longer pieces.
options.motion: Deliberate pacing, zooms into controls, highlight rings pulse on the next target, pauses long enough to read.
options.use: Help centers, YouTube, docs, customer education.
options.conveys: Competence and patience; the viewer can follow along.
options.vs: A feature walkthrough is shorter and lighter on explanation; an educational explainer teaches concepts rather than product tasks.
options.prompt: Pace for following along: each step gets a caption stating the action, a highlight ring on the target control, the action, then a hold of >= 2 s on the result. Use zoom insets (2x) for small controls. No step shorter than 4 s; no more than one new UI element introduced per step.

options.what: Shows how work flows across steps, tools or people using the product, emphasizing handoffs and automation.
options.looks: Multiple panels or apps connected by lines, arrows or moving cards; status chips changing; avatars for people.
options.motion: Objects travel between panels; state changes cascade; connectors draw on as data moves.
options.use: Automation and integration products, B2B platform marketing, use-case pages.
options.vs: A process visualization is abstract and product-agnostic; a workflow demonstration uses the product's real surfaces. A feature walkthrough stays inside one screen.
options.prompt: Lay out 3-5 stages left-to-right or as a loop, each a simplified product card. Move one object (a task, message, file) through the stages; at each handoff draw a connector (300-500 ms stroke-on) and flip a status chip. Keep the traveling object visually identical across stages so the eye tracks it.

options.what: Shows a state without the product and the improved state with it, side by side or in sequence.
options.looks: Two matched frames: the 'before' desaturated, cluttered or red-tinted; the 'after' clean and brand-colored; labels 'Before'/'After'.
options.motion: Wipe or slider reveal between states, morph of the same layout, or split screen with a dividing line that sweeps.
options.use: Ads, landing pages, redesign announcements, performance claims.
options.vs: A comparison animation pits the product against competitors or options; before/after compares the same subject over time.
options.prompt: Match the framing of both states exactly so only the change reads. Show 'before' first for 1.5-2.5 s (muted color, cluttered), then reveal 'after' with a vertical wipe or slider sweep over 600-900 ms, and hold 'after' >= 2 s. Label each state in a small caption.

options.what: Contrasts two or more options (products, plans, methods) on the same criteria.
options.looks: Split screen or columns, checkmarks and crosses, bars or metrics side by side, one side highlighted in brand color.
options.motion: Criteria appear row by row; values tick up in parallel; the winning side lights up or grows.
options.use: Competitive ads, pricing pages, migration campaigns.
options.vs: Before/after compares one subject over time; comparison compares different subjects at the same time.
options.prompt: Use a two-column split with identical row structure. Reveal one criterion at a time (600-900 ms per row, stagger 150 ms between columns), then highlight the preferred option's column in the accent color at the end. Keep competitors neutral gray, not ugly; the argument is the data.

options.what: A digest of several recent improvements, shown as a quick sequence of small reveals.
options.looks: Version number or date header, list of items each with a mini UI clip or icon, consistent card template.
options.motion: Rapid card-to-card rhythm, each item gets 2-4 s, a counter or list progress indicator.
options.use: Monthly update posts, product newsletters, community channels.
options.conveys: Steady momentum; a team that ships.
options.vs: A feature reveal gives one item full attention; a changelog animation gives many items equal, brief attention.
options.prompt: Open with the version or month as a title card (1.5 s). Present 4-8 items in one repeating template: item title, a 2-4 s mini demo or icon animation, one-line benefit. Keep transitions identical between items (e.g. 400 ms horizontal slide) and show a progress indicator such as '3/6'.

options.what: A silent, looping or single-play animation that sits in a website's hero area and carries the product idea above the fold.
options.looks: Composed to leave room for the headline and CTA; product UI or abstract visual; restrained color; no burned-in text or minimal text.
options.motion: Continuous and calm, seamless loop 6-20 s, no hard cuts, no flashing; motion concentrated away from the text column.
options.use: Homepages, product pages, feature sections.
options.conveys: Instant product comprehension and polish without demanding attention.
options.vs: A product demo is watched deliberately with sound; a hero animation is glanced at, silent, and must loop. A motion background has no product content.
options.prompt: Make a silent 8-15 s seamless loop sized for a web hero (16:9 or wider). Keep the left or top 40% calm for the site's headline; concentrate motion in the product area. No hard cuts, no flashes, nothing that reads as an ending; the last frame must match the first exactly.

options.what: A short, vertical-first video showing an app's key screens for store listings.
options.looks: Device-framed or full-bleed app screens, big captions above or below, bright brand backgrounds.
options.motion: Fast screen-to-screen swipes, taps and scrolls mirroring real use, 2-4 s per screen.
options.use: Apple App Store app previews, Google Play promo videos, app install ads.
options.conveys: The app is useful and easy at a glance.
options.vs: A UI showcase is for designers; an app-store promo is for downloaders and must follow store rules (Apple app previews must show actual app footage, 15-30 s).
options.prompt: Make a 15-30 s vertical (9:16) piece of 5-8 screens. Each screen: a 3-6 word caption in large type, then real in-app interaction (tap, scroll, swipe) at realistic speed; 2.5-4 s per screen. Open on the single most valuable screen, not a splash screen.

options.what: An animation that builds or unveils a logo, usually 3-10 s, ending on the static mark.
options.looks: The logo assembled from its own geometry, drawn on, unmasked or formed from particles; clean background.
options.motion: Anticipation, build, settle; a final resolve where motion stops fully and the mark holds.
options.use: Video intros and outros, presentations, brand launches.
options.conveys: Identity and arrival; the brand's personality in one gesture.
options.vs: A logo sting is shorter (1-3 s) and punchier, often with sound; a logo reveal can be longer and more elaborate. An ident is a broadcast channel identifier with a scene around the logo.
options.prompt: Animate the logo from its own construction (strokes drawing on, shapes assembling, or a mask revealing letterforms) over 2-4 s, then a settle of 300-600 ms and a full stop. Hold the finished static logo >= 1.5 s. Never distort the final mark's proportions or color.

options.what: A very short (1-3 s) punchy logo animation, typically paired with a sonic logo, used to punctuate content.
options.looks: Logo snaps in with one strong gesture; minimal or no scene around it.
options.motion: Fast in, overshoot or impact, immediate hold; tightly synced to a sound hit.
options.use: End of ads, YouTube pre-roll tags, transitions between segments, social video outros.
options.vs: Logo reveal is longer and more constructive. 'Bumper' in broadcast means a short clip between program and break, which may not be a logo at all; terminology is loose.
options.prompt: Make a 1.5-2.5 s sting: one decisive gesture (snap, slice, stamp or spin) that lands the full logo by 0.8 s, synced to a single audio hit, then hold still to the end. No multi-step build; one idea only.

options.what: A brand identity whose logo and core elements are designed to move, with defined animated behaviours.
options.looks: Logo with states or variations, brand shapes that transform, consistent color and type.
options.motion: Signature behaviors: a specific way the mark forms, reacts or transitions; repeatable across uses.
options.use: Rebrands, product brands, digital-first companies.
options.vs: A motion identity system is the full rulebook (easing, timing, transitions, typography motion) across all touchpoints; an animated identity is primarily the moving logo and its core assets.
options.prompt: Define 3 core animated behaviors for the logo (form, idle, exit) using its geometry, each 0.8-2.5 s, and show them in sequence with the same easing curve. Demonstrate the mark in 2-3 contexts (dark, light, small size) to show the behavior holds.

options.what: A codified set of motion principles, easing curves, durations, transitions and components that make all of a brand's motion feel related.
options.looks: Presented as a system: easing curve diagrams, timing scales, component examples, do/don't pairs, applied mockups.
options.motion: Every example uses the same small vocabulary of curves and durations; transitions and type behaviors repeat.
options.use: Brand guidelines, design systems, agency rebrand deliverables.
options.vs: An animated identity is the logo moving; a motion identity system governs everything that moves, including UI.
options.prompt: Present the motion system in chapters: 1) principles (3 words, each demonstrated in 3-4 s), 2) easing curves shown as plotted graphs with a dot tracing them, 3) duration scale (e.g. 150/250/400/600/900 ms) with side-by-side examples, 4) transitions and type behaviors, 5) applied examples. Every example uses only the defined curves and durations.

options.what: A longer-form piece (60-180 s) about what a company believes and why it exists, often light on product.
options.looks: Cinematic framing, footage or rich illustration, big emotive typography, restrained brand presence until the end.
options.motion: Slower, emotive pacing, music-led, sweeping camera, typography that breathes.
options.use: Rebrands, company homepages, recruiting, events.
options.vs: A manifesto film is text- or voice-led and declarative; a brand film can be narrative. A launch film sells a product; a brand film sells the company.
options.prompt: Build a 60-120 s film led by music and one line of narrative voice per scene. Open on an image or statement that states the tension, develop 3-4 scenes showing the belief in the world, withhold the logo until the final 5-8 s. Holds of 3-6 s per shot; no feature lists.

options.what: A short broadcast or platform piece (5-30 s) that identifies a channel or brand, typically a small scene built around the logo.
options.looks: A self-contained world or vignette where the logo appears or is formed; series of variations sharing one concept.
options.motion: A mini-story or loopable scene resolving on the logo; often designed as a family of variants.
options.use: TV channels, streaming platforms, event broadcasts, conference sessions.
options.vs: A logo sting is only the logo gesture; an ident is a scene with the logo in it. Informally 'ident' is also used for any logo animation in UK usage.
options.prompt: Design a 6-10 s ident: one self-contained scene with a single visual idea that resolves into the logo in the final 2 s. Build it so 2-3 variants can share the idea with different subjects. Keep the logo in a consistent position and scale across variants.

options.what: A set of animated assets built around one campaign idea and deployed across channels and formats.
options.looks: One key visual and line adapted to many aspect ratios and durations; consistent campaign typography and color.
options.motion: A signature transition or motif repeated across all cutdowns; modular so parts can be re-cut.
options.use: Seasonal campaigns, launches, out-of-home digital screens, paid social.
options.conveys: A unified message with presence everywhere.
options.vs: A brand film is one piece; campaign animation is a system of pieces. Social ad is one deliverable within a campaign.
options.prompt: Build around one campaign line and one key visual. Design the master (15-30 s, 16:9) with a repeatable signature motif, then structure scenes as modules so 6 s and 15 s cutdowns and 9:16 / 1:1 versions can be made by re-ordering and re-framing, not redesigning.

options.what: A declarative piece that states a brand's beliefs as a series of bold lines, usually typography- or voice-led.
options.looks: Large statement typography, strong contrast, few colors, lines filling the frame one at a time, sometimes with footage behind.
options.motion: Rhythmic line-by-line delivery, cuts on the beat or on each phrase, rising intensity to a final statement.
options.use: Rebrands, company launches, recruiting, conference openers.
options.vs: A brand film can be narrative or observational; a manifesto is a direct statement. A typographic statement is a single line; a manifesto is a sequence of them.
options.prompt: Write 6-10 short declarative lines (3-8 words each). Present one line per beat in large type (>= 8% of frame height), each held long enough to read twice (~1 s per 3 words + 0.5 s). Build intensity: faster cuts and larger type toward the end, then a final line and logo held >= 2 s.

options.what: Ongoing, template-driven branded motion for social feeds: quotes, tips, announcements, stats in a consistent style.
options.looks: Consistent frame template, brand colors and fonts, logo corner bug, 1:1, 4:5 or 9:16.
options.motion: Short, repeatable text and shape animations; same in/out behaviors every post.
options.use: Instagram, LinkedIn, TikTok, X brand accounts.
options.conveys: Consistency and recognizability in the feed.
options.vs: A social ad is paid and conversion-focused; brand social content is organic, recurring and template-based.
options.prompt: Design a reusable template: fixed safe margins, logo bug in one corner, one text style for headline and one for body. Animate text in with the same 400-600 ms behavior each time, hold the message >= 3 s, and loop or end cleanly within 6-12 s. Must read with sound off.

options.what: Explains an abstract idea or mental model rather than a product or procedure.
options.looks: Diagrams, simple shapes, icons and metaphors; minimal UI; clear labels.
options.motion: Build-up diagrams, elements that transform to show relationships, progressive reveals.
options.use: Thought leadership, onboarding to a new category, education.
options.vs: A product explainer ties the idea to the product; a concept explainer is product-agnostic. A metaphor-led explainer is one technique for a concept explainer.
options.prompt: Explain one idea in 3-5 beats, each adding exactly one new element to a persistent diagram (the frame accumulates rather than resets). Label every element when it appears; hold each completed state >= 2 s before adding the next.

options.what: Explains what a product is, who it's for and how it works, usually 60-120 s with voiceover.
options.looks: Mix of illustration or simplified UI and headline cards; often a character or scenario; brand palette.
options.motion: Problem scene, product introduction, 3 benefit scenes, CTA; transitions follow the script.
options.use: Homepages, sales outreach, investor decks.
options.vs: A product demo shows the product working; an explainer explains why and how it helps, often with illustration rather than real UI.
options.prompt: Structure 60-90 s as: problem (10-15 s), product introduced (5-10 s), how it works in 3 steps (30-40 s), benefits and proof (10-15 s), CTA (5 s). One scene per script sentence; every UI shown is simplified to the one element the line mentions.

options.what: Explains a sequence of stages (manufacturing, a pipeline, a service journey) in order.
options.looks: Stepped layout, numbered stages, arrows or conveyor paths, consistent icon style.
options.motion: Left-to-right or top-to-bottom travel, one stage activating at a time, a token moving through.
options.use: Service businesses, technical products, compliance and ops communication.
options.vs: Process visualization is a single diagram animation; a process explainer is a full narrated piece around it. Workflow demonstration uses real product UI.
options.prompt: Show 3-6 stages on a single path. Activate one stage at a time (highlight + label + 1-line description), move a token along the connector between stages over 600-1000 ms, and keep completed stages visible but dimmed to 40% so the whole process is readable at the end.

options.what: Motion designed to teach a subject (science, history, finance) with retention in mind.
options.looks: Illustrations, diagrams, labeled visuals, chapter titles, recap cards.
options.motion: Measured pacing, repetition of key visuals, visual mnemonics, recaps.
options.use: YouTube channels, e-learning, museums, classroom content.
options.vs: A tutorial teaches a task in a tool; educational motion teaches knowledge. Concept explainers are usually commercial; educational motion is usually not.
options.prompt: Teach one topic in chapters of 30-60 s, each opening with a title card and ending with a one-line recap. Reuse the same visual for the same concept every time it recurs. Introduce at most one new term per 10 s and label it on screen when spoken.

options.what: Explains how a technical system works (architecture, protocols, APIs, algorithms) for a technical audience.
options.looks: System diagrams, code snippets, terminals, packets and nodes, monospace labels, dark themes common.
options.motion: Data packets moving along edges, code typing or highlighting line by line, layers exploding apart.
options.use: Developer tools marketing, conference talks, docs, engineering blogs.
options.vs: Diagram-led explainer is a technique; technical explainer is defined by audience and subject. Avoid over-simplifying: engineers distrust vague diagrams.
options.prompt: Use accurate system diagrams with real component names and monospace labels. Show data flow as small packets traveling along edges at constant speed; highlight code line by line in sync with the diagram. Keep the diagram persistent and zoom into subsystems rather than cutting away.

options.what: An explainer where an evolving diagram is the main visual, built up and annotated as the argument proceeds.
options.looks: Line-based diagrams, flat shapes, arrows, labels, a lot of negative space; often a single canvas.
options.motion: Stroke-on lines, elements appearing in logical order, camera pans across a large canvas.
options.use: Concept and technical explainers, strategy presentations.
options.vs: Whiteboard animation (hand drawing on white) is a specific style of diagram-led explainer; not all diagram-led work looks hand-drawn.
options.prompt: Build one large diagram on a single canvas; draw each element on in the order of the argument (strokes 400-800 ms), label as it appears, and move the camera across the canvas rather than cutting. End by pulling back to show the full diagram for >= 3 s.

options.what: Explains an abstract idea through a concrete visual metaphor (a pipeline as plumbing, security as a lock, data as water).
options.looks: Illustrated or 3D objects standing in for abstractions, sometimes morphing into the real thing at the end.
options.motion: Metaphor objects behave physically; transformations map metaphor to reality.
options.use: Brand and product explainers for non-technical audiences.
options.vs: A diagram-led explainer is literal and structural; a metaphor-led one borrows a familiar system. Risk: metaphors that don't map cleanly confuse.
options.prompt: Pick one metaphor and keep it for the whole piece (never mix metaphors). Establish it in the first scene, let every later beat extend the same object's behavior, then in the final beat morph the metaphor object into the real product or UI element it stood for.

options.what: Animated text as the main visual, with type moving expressively in time with speech or music.
options.looks: Words and phrases filling the frame, varied scale and weight for emphasis, few or no images.
options.motion: Words enter on syllables or beats; scale, rotation and position shifts emphasize meaning; camera often travels through a type layout.
options.use: Promos, lyric videos, manifestos, social video, talks.
options.conveys: Energy and emphasis; the words are the message.
options.vs: A typographic statement is one static-leaning line; kinetic typography is continuous motion across many words. 'Kinetic type' is often used loosely for any animated text.
options.prompt: Make type the only primary visual. Animate word-by-word or phrase-by-phrase in time with voice or beat; vary scale by meaning (key words 2-4x body size, heavier weight). Reposition the camera or grid between phrases so no two consecutive phrases share the same layout.

options.what: A single line or short phrase animated as a hero moment, then held.
options.looks: One large headline, carefully set, lots of negative space; possibly one supporting element.
options.motion: Precise, restrained build (line reveal, mask, weight shift) followed by a long hold.
options.use: Launch films, ads, social posts, presentation openers.
options.vs: Kinetic typography keeps moving; a typographic statement arrives and stays.
options.prompt: Set one line of 2-8 words at display size (>= 10% of frame height), reveal it with a single mask or line-by-line wipe over 600-1000 ms, then hold perfectly still for >= 2 s. Nothing else moves.

options.what: Animates a quotation or testimonial with attribution.
options.looks: Quote marks as graphic device, body text set for reading, name, role, photo or logo for attribution.
options.motion: Text reveals by line at reading speed, attribution fades in last, subtle drift during hold.
options.use: Customer testimonials, social posts, case studies, press quotes.
options.vs: A typographic statement is the brand speaking; a quote animation is someone else speaking.
options.prompt: Reveal the quote line by line at reading pace (~200 ms per word minimum on screen before the next line), then bring in attribution (name, role, logo or headshot) 400 ms after the final line. Hold the complete quote for at least as long as it took to reveal.

options.what: Song lyrics animated in sync with the vocal, as the primary visual of a music video or clip.
options.looks: Lyrics large and stylized to the song's mood; background imagery optional.
options.motion: Word-level sync to the vocal, emphasis on hooks, chorus visually distinct from verses.
options.use: Music releases, social clips, fan content.
options.vs: Kinetic typography can follow any audio; lyric animation is locked to sung words and song structure (verse, chorus, bridge).
options.prompt: Sync each word to its sung onset (+/- 1 frame). Give verses one layout and treatment, the chorus a bigger, repeated treatment that returns identically each time. Do not show upcoming lines early.

options.what: A short ad where copy carries the whole pitch, typically for sound-off social feeds.
options.looks: Bold, high-contrast type, few words per card, brand color fields, CTA at the end.
options.motion: Punchy card-to-card cuts or snaps, 1-2 s per card, occasional product flash.
options.use: Paid social, display, digital out-of-home.
options.vs: Kinetic typography is expressive; a text-led ad is functional copy delivery optimized for conversion.
options.prompt: Write 4-7 cards of <= 6 words each. Show each card 1-2 s with a hard cut or 200 ms snap between; one card must state the offer and the last card is the CTA + logo held >= 2 s. Max two type weights and two colors.

options.what: An infographic brought to life: icons, numbers, charts and short text combined to tell a factual story.
options.looks: Icons, pictograms, big numbers, simple charts, consistent grid and palette.
options.motion: Sequential builds, count-ups, icons popping in, charts growing, one fact per beat.
options.use: Reports, social posts, internal comms, journalism.
options.vs: Data visualization emphasizes accurate encoding of datasets; an infographic mixes illustration, icons and a few numbers for storytelling.
options.prompt: Tell 4-6 facts, one per beat. Each beat pairs one number or chart with one icon and one short label; numbers count up over 800-1200 ms, then hold >= 1.5 s. Use a fixed grid and one icon style throughout.

options.what: Motion that encodes real data accurately in charts, plots or visual encodings.
options.looks: Axes, bars, lines, points, labels, legends; restrained color used to encode categories.
options.motion: Values animate from a true baseline; transitions between chart states preserve object identity; annotations appear when relevant.
options.use: Reports, journalism, investor updates, analytics products.
options.vs: Statistics animation highlights a few hero numbers; data visualization shows the shape of the data. An infographic may bend accuracy for storytelling; dataviz should not.
options.prompt: Encode real values accurately: bars grow from a zero baseline, lines draw left to right in time order, axes and labels appear before data. When the chart changes state, morph the same marks rather than replacing them. Annotate the single key insight with a callout and hold >= 2 s.

options.what: Animates one or a few headline numbers for impact.
options.looks: Huge numerals, a short descriptor, maybe a supporting icon or mini chart.
options.motion: Count-up or odometer roll, scale emphasis on landing, supporting label follows.
options.use: Launch films, annual reports, social proof sections, sales decks.
options.vs: Data visualization shows relationships across many values; statistics animation spotlights a single number.
options.prompt: Show one number at a time at display size (>= 20% frame height) with tabular figures. Count up over 1-1.5 s with ease-out so it decelerates onto the final value, bring the descriptor in 200 ms after landing, hold >= 1.5 s.

options.what: Animates geography: locations, routes, regions or spatial data.
options.looks: Stylized or satellite maps, pins, routes, highlighted regions, labels.
options.motion: Zooms from global to local, routes drawing on, regions filling, pins dropping.
options.use: Expansion announcements, logistics, travel, journalism, event content.
options.vs: Network visualization shows abstract connections; a map animation is geographically true.
options.prompt: Start wide to establish context, then zoom continuously (no cuts) to the region of interest over 2-3 s. Draw routes with a stroke-on and a leading dot; drop pins with a short settle; label places in one consistent style. Use a desaturated base map with the accent color reserved for the data.

options.what: Presents events in chronological order along a time axis.
options.looks: A line or track with dates, milestone markers, images or captions per event.
options.motion: Camera tracks along the line; markers activate as the playhead passes; year counters.
options.use: Company history, product evolution, anniversaries, case studies.
options.vs: A process visualization shows stages of how something works; a timeline shows when things happened.
options.prompt: Draw one horizontal (or vertical for 9:16) time axis. Track the camera along it at a steady pace; at each milestone, the marker activates, the date appears in large type and a caption or image follows, held 1.5-3 s. Show a running year counter if the span is long.

options.what: An animated diagram of a process or pipeline, usually abstract and self-contained.
options.looks: Nodes, stages, arrows, conveyor paths, flow lines.
options.motion: Tokens flow through stages, stages light up in sequence, looping flows.
options.use: Inside explainers, landing page sections, docs.
options.vs: A process explainer is a full narrated piece; a process visualization is one diagram-level animation. Network visualization has no fixed order.
options.prompt: Draw the process as nodes connected by paths, then send tokens through at constant speed, lighting each stage as the token passes (150-250 ms highlight). Loop seamlessly by timing the next token to enter as the last exits.

options.what: Animates relationships between many entities as nodes and edges.
options.looks: Nodes (dots, avatars, logos) linked by lines; clusters; glowing or pulsing connections.
options.motion: Nodes appear and connect progressively, force-directed settling, pulses traveling along edges.
options.use: Platforms, integrations pages, social and security products, infrastructure.
options.vs: Process visualization is ordered; network visualization is relational. Map animation is geographic.
options.prompt: Start with one central node, then spawn connected nodes in waves (stagger 40-80 ms) with edges drawing out from the center. Let the layout settle with a gentle spring, then send small pulses along a few edges to show activity. Limit to 20-60 nodes so it stays legible.

options.what: Animates a dashboard of metrics, charts and widgets populating with data.
options.looks: Card grid of KPIs, charts, tables; product-accurate or simplified.
options.motion: Cards assemble in a stagger, numbers count up, charts draw, live-data ticks.
options.use: Analytics, fintech and ops product marketing, landing heroes.
options.vs: Data visualization focuses on one chart's story; dashboard animation shows many metrics as a product surface. Overlaps with UI showcase.
options.prompt: Assemble the dashboard in a stagger (cards 60-100 ms apart, top-left to bottom-right), then populate: KPIs count up, charts draw over 800-1200 ms. Afterward, make one metric update live and zoom to it to deliver the insight.

options.what: A designed sequence presenting a film's or series' title and credits while setting its tone.
options.looks: Cinematic, concept-driven imagery, carefully set credits, a strong visual metaphor for the story.
options.motion: Paced to a score; credits appear in rhythm; transitions carry the metaphor.
options.use: Film, TV series, games, conferences with cinematic ambitions.
options.vs: Opening titles are the credits at the start (may be over action); a title sequence is a standalone designed piece. End titles are the closing credits.
refs: Catch Me If You Can title sequence
options.prompt: Build a 60-120 s sequence around one visual metaphor for the story. Present 6-12 credits, each held 2-3 s in one consistent typographic treatment, timed to the score's phrases. End on the title card, larger and held >= 3 s.

options.what: Credits and title that open a production, either as a standalone sequence or overlaid on the opening scene.
options.looks: Credit text over footage or designed backgrounds; restrained type in a fixed position style.
options.motion: Credits fade or reveal gently, synced to scene rhythm; title card as climax.
options.use: Films, series, documentaries, conference opens.
options.vs: A title sequence is a fully designed standalone piece; opening titles may just be credits over action. 'Open' in broadcast also means a show's recurring intro package.
options.prompt: Overlay 4-8 credits on footage or a designed background, each in the same position system (e.g. lower third or center), fading or masking in over 500-800 ms, held 2-3 s. Build to the title card, which gets its own reveal and a 3 s hold.

options.what: The closing credits or end card: a list of contributors or a final branded frame.
options.looks: Credit roll or designed end-title cards; logos, legal lines.
options.motion: Steady vertical roll at constant speed or card sequences; minimal motion.
options.use: Films, series, brand films, events.
options.vs: Opening titles set tone; end titles close and credit. In ads, 'end card' means the final CTA/logo frame.
options.prompt: Roll credits at constant speed (each line on screen >= 2 s) in two columns (role / name) with consistent leading, or present end cards held 2-3 s each. Keep type small and quiet; finish on logo and copyright line held >= 2 s.

options.what: A coordinated set of on-air graphics for a show or channel: open, bumpers, transitions, lower thirds, full-screens, end slate.
options.looks: One design system repeated across many elements; safe-area aware; designed for live data insertion.
options.motion: Repeatable in/out animations of fixed durations, transitions (stingers) that cover cuts.
options.use: TV, live streams, esports, corporate broadcasts, conferences.
options.vs: A single ident is one element; a broadcast package is the full kit. Informally just 'the package'.
options.prompt: Design a kit that shares one system: show open (10-15 s), transition stinger (1-1.5 s, fully covering the frame at its midpoint), lower third, full-screen info card, and end slate. Each element has identical in (400-600 ms) and out (300-500 ms) behaviors and respects title-safe margins.

options.what: A graphic in the lower portion of the frame identifying a speaker, location or topic.
options.looks: Name and title on a bar or clean text block, sitting in the bottom third within title-safe.
options.motion: Quick, unobtrusive in (300-600 ms), hold, out; lines or bars wipe on before text.
options.use: Interviews, talks, news, webinars, documentaries, social video.
options.vs: 'Chyron' is a US broadcast term (from the Chyron company) often used for any on-screen text in news; lower third specifically names position.
options.prompt: Place in the lower-left third within title-safe. Animate a bar or rule wiping on (250 ms), name sliding up from a mask (300 ms), title 100 ms after; hold 4-6 s; exit in 300 ms in reverse. Name weight bold, title regular at 60-70% size.

options.what: On-air graphics for sports: scorebugs, player cards, stats, line-ups, replays transitions.
options.looks: High-energy, bold condensed type, team colors, angular shapes, player cutouts, metallic or glassy materials.
options.motion: Aggressive, fast transitions, light sweeps, slams and snaps, stat bars filling.
options.use: Live sports, esports, fantasy apps, team social.
options.vs: News graphics prioritize neutrality and clarity; sports graphics prioritize energy and team identity.
options.prompt: Use bold condensed type, team colors and angular shapes. Player or stat cards slam in (200-300 ms, strong ease-out), a light sweep crosses once, stats fill as bars over 500 ms. Hold each card 3-4 s and exit with a fast diagonal wipe.

options.what: Graphics for news: headlines, tickers, maps, explainer full-screens, breaking-news bumpers.
options.looks: Clear hierarchy, sober palette with a signal color (often red for breaking), sans-serif type, data panels.
options.motion: Crisp, efficient, minimal flourish; tickers scroll at constant speed; urgent stingers for breaking news.
options.use: Broadcast news, digital news video, explainers.
options.vs: Sports graphics are energetic and partisan; news graphics are neutral and restrained.
options.prompt: Use a sober palette with one signal color, a clear sans-serif, and a strict layout grid. Keep transitions short (250-400 ms) and functional; tickers scroll at constant speed; full-screen cards hold >= 5 s for reading.

options.what: Visuals driven by or tightly synced to music's amplitude, frequencies and beats.
options.looks: Waveforms, spectrum bars, pulsing shapes, particles, cover art or artist name.
options.motion: Audio-reactive: scale, glow and displacement following kick, snare and bass; loops.
options.use: Music releases, Spotify Canvas, streams, live shows.
options.vs: Lyric animation shows words; a visualizer shows sound itself. VJ loops are for live performance.
options.prompt: Map audio features to properties: kick drum -> scale pulse (+6-10%, 80 ms attack, 300 ms decay), bass energy -> background glow, high frequencies -> particle emission. Keep a stable central composition (cover art or title) so the reactive motion reads against it.

options.what: A high-impact video that opens an event, conference or keynote and builds anticipation.
options.looks: Large-scale, cinematic, event branding, big type, often screen-wall formats.
options.motion: Build with rising energy, countdowns, a hero reveal of the event name.
options.use: Conferences, product keynotes, award shows, all-hands.
options.vs: A title sequence introduces a story; an event opener introduces a live moment and hands off to a presenter.
options.prompt: Build a 45-90 s piece in three acts: atmospheric setup (quiet, slow), escalating montage of themes or speakers (cuts accelerate from 2 s to 0.5 s), and the event name reveal on the musical peak, held >= 4 s to hand off to the stage.

options.what: A short paid ad designed for social feeds, optimized for thumb-stopping and conversion.
options.looks: Vertical or square, big captions, product in the first second, brand visible early, CTA end card.
options.motion: Instant hook in 0-1 s, fast pacing, pattern interrupts every 1-2 s, legible with sound off.
options.use: Meta, TikTok, YouTube Shorts, LinkedIn, Snap.
options.vs: Brand social content is organic and recurring; a social ad is paid and measured. A teaser withholds info; a social ad states the offer.
options.prompt: Make a 6-15 s vertical (9:16) ad. Show the product or hook in frame 1, change the visual every 1-1.5 s, caption every spoken line (text inside the central 70% safe zone), state the offer by 5 s, end with CTA + logo held 2 s. Must work with sound off.

options.what: A short piece that announces news: funding, partnership, hire, milestone, event date.
options.looks: Headline-first, logos (for partnerships), key number or date large, brand template.
options.motion: One strong reveal of the news, supporting details, logo sign-off.
options.use: LinkedIn, X, company blogs, press kits.
options.vs: A feature reveal announces product capability; an announcement animation announces company or event news.
options.prompt: Make 8-15 s: a 1 s anticipation beat, the news headline revealed boldly (<= 8 words), one supporting detail (number, date, partner logo lockup with a '+' or '×'), then brand sign-off. Hold the headline >= 2.5 s.

options.what: A short piece that withholds most information to build curiosity before a launch.
options.looks: Dark or cropped framing, fragments of product, silhouettes, glints, cryptic line, date.
options.motion: Slow reveals interrupted by cuts, partial glimpses, macro details, a date slam at the end.
options.use: Pre-launch social, countdown campaigns, event build-up.
options.vs: A trailer shows more and follows a structure (setup, escalation, title); a teaser deliberately shows almost nothing. Marketing teams use the terms interchangeably.
options.prompt: Make 6-20 s. Show only fragments: extreme crops, silhouettes, edges catching light, never the whole product or UI. Low-key lighting, slow moves broken by 1-3 frame flash cuts. End on a cryptic line and a date, held 2 s.

options.what: A structured promotional piece that previews a product, event or content with escalating energy.
options.looks: Title cards between shots, montage of highlights, big type, climactic title and date.
options.motion: Three-act trailer structure: setup, escalation with faster cuts, climax and title; music-driven with hits and drops.
options.use: Product launches, games, events, content series.
options.vs: A teaser withholds; a trailer reveals highlights. A launch film may be calmer and more explanatory.
options.prompt: Structure 30-90 s in three acts: act 1 establishes (shots 2-3 s), act 2 escalates (shots 0.5-1.5 s, title cards on musical hits), a beat of silence, then the climax with the name and date held >= 3 s.

options.what: Very short promotional motion (6-15 s), often cut down from a longer piece.
options.looks: One idea, one product shot, one line, logo.
options.motion: Economical: every second carries the message; rapid build to sign-off.
options.use: YouTube 6 s bumpers, story placements, pre-roll.
options.vs: A social ad can be longer and conversion-heavy; short-form promo is about one-idea recall. 'Bumper ad' is YouTube's 6 s non-skippable format.
options.prompt: Make 6 s (or 10-15 s max) with one idea: hook in 0-1 s, message in 1-4 s, logo and line held from 4 s to end. No more than 10 words on screen in total.

options.what: Real footage cut into a vertical social reel with graphics, captions and music.
options.looks: Vertical 9:16 footage, bold captions or text overlays, occasional graphic stickers, color grade.
options.motion: Beat-cut edits, speed ramps, punch-in zooms, kinetic captions, jump cuts.
options.use: Instagram Reels, TikTok, YouTube Shorts, event and product recaps.
options.conveys: Authenticity and energy; native to the feed.
options.vs: A social ad is paid and can be fully animated; a reel is footage-first and can be organic. A recap covers a specific event.
options.prompt: Cut footage to 9:16, 15-45 s. Hook in the first 1 s (the strongest shot or a question caption). Cut on beats, 0.6-2 s per shot, use punch-in zooms (110-130%) for emphasis and speed ramps into key moments. Keep captions in the central safe zone, clear of the platform UI at the bottom 20%.

options.what: A montage summarizing an event, year or campaign through its best moments.
options.looks: Footage of crowds, speakers and details; overlaid stats, names and dates; branded frames.
options.motion: Montage cut to music, building energy, stat callouts, closing logo and 'see you next year'.
options.use: Conferences, launches, year-in-review, internal all-hands.
options.vs: A reel can be about anything; a recap is retrospective about one event or period. 'Sizzle reel' is informal and also used for pitch montages.
options.prompt: Cut 45-90 s of footage to music in three phases: arrival and atmosphere (2-3 s shots), peak moments montage (0.5-1.5 s shots on beats), and a close with 2-4 stat callouts (attendees, sessions, countries) and the logo. Overlay speaker names as lower thirds when faces are shown.

options.what: A short animation whose last frame flows seamlessly into its first, designed to repeat indefinitely.
options.looks: Self-contained composition, cyclic motion, no beginning or end cues.
options.motion: Cyclical: rotations, oscillations, conveyor motion, periodic transformations with matched start/end states.
options.use: Social posts, web sections, displays, Dribbble.
options.vs: GIF-style motion is a loop constrained by GIF aesthetics; a motion background is a loop that plays behind content.
options.prompt: Make a 3-8 s loop where every animated property returns exactly to its starting value on the last frame (use full periods: 360° rotations, whole sine cycles). Avoid anything that reads as a start or end: no fades from black, no title cards.

options.what: Tiny, punchy, looping animation in the GIF idiom: short, limited palette, instantly readable.
options.looks: Flat colors, bold shapes, limited frames, sometimes stepped/choppy timing, small canvas.
options.motion: 1-3 s loops, snappy repetitive action, sometimes 12 fps stepped timing.
options.use: Slack/Giphy stickers, newsletters, docs, reactions, README headers.
options.vs: A loop can be long and cinematic; GIF-style motion is small, short and punchy with limited color by design.
options.prompt: Make a 1-3 s loop, flat colors (<= 6), bold simple shapes, a single repeated action. Optionally step the timing to 12 fps for a hand-made feel. Readable at 240 px wide.

options.what: A subtle, seamless animated background that supports content placed on top of it.
options.looks: Gradients, soft shapes, particles, textures; low contrast; no focal point.
options.motion: Slow, continuous drift, no sudden changes; seamless loop 10-60 s.
options.use: Websites, presentations, streams, video backdrops, lock screens.
options.vs: A generative background runs procedurally without a fixed loop; a motion background is usually a rendered loop. A hero animation carries product content.
options.prompt: Make a 15-30 s seamless loop with low contrast (keep luminance variation within ~15%), no focal point and slow drift (nothing crosses the frame faster than 1/10 of its width per second). Leave legible space for foreground text.

options.what: Long-duration, idle-state motion designed to run unattended on a screen.
options.looks: Slowly evolving scenes, brand imagery, clocks or info; burn-in aware (nothing static for long).
options.motion: Very slow, continuous change; no cuts; subtle position shifts to avoid burn-in.
options.use: Devices, kiosks, retail displays, office screens.
options.vs: A motion background supports foreground content; a screensaver is the whole show when nothing else happens. An attract loop in retail/arcade usage is meant to draw people in, so it has more action.
options.prompt: Design a long, slowly evolving loop (60 s+) with no static element held in place longer than ~30 s. Motion extremely slow and continuous, no cuts or flashes. If showing brand or time, drift its position gently over the loop.

options.what: Motion made for physical spaces: projection, LED walls, immersive rooms, unusual canvases.
options.looks: Non-standard aspect ratios, very large scale, often abstract or generative, architecture-aware.
options.motion: Slow, immersive, sometimes interactive or sensor-driven; designed to be viewed from distance and in motion.
options.use: Museums, retail flagships, events, lobbies, exhibitions.
options.vs: An event backdrop supports a stage program; an installation is the experience itself.
options.prompt: Design for the physical canvas (state its exact aspect and pixel size, e.g. 7680x1080). Use large, slow forms legible from 5-20 m; avoid small text; motion evolves over minutes. Specify how the piece loops or responds to presence.

options.what: Procedurally generated visuals (noise fields, particles, flow fields, shaders) that evolve in real time.
options.looks: Organic, never-quite-repeating patterns: flow fields, noise gradients, particle swarms, meshes.
options.motion: Continuous, rule-based, often seeded or data/audio-reactive.
options.use: Web heroes, events, installations, brand systems.
options.vs: A motion background is a fixed rendered loop; generative visuals come from rules and can run indefinitely. For deterministic rendering, seed the randomness.
options.prompt: Generate visuals from a seeded rule system (e.g. Perlin/simplex noise flow field driving 2,000-8,000 particles, or a noise-warped gradient shader). Keep speed slow and palette limited to 2-4 brand colors. Use a fixed seed so every render is deterministic.

options.what: Stage-screen motion that runs behind presenters or performers during an event.
options.looks: Branded, low-distraction loops; wide or unusual formats; speaker-safe zones.
options.motion: Slow ambient loops with occasional cue-based transitions (walk-on, applause).
options.use: Conferences, keynotes, concerts, award shows.
options.vs: An event opener is a one-off hero video; an event backdrop runs for hours as supporting visuals.
options.prompt: Make wide-format (e.g. 32:9) loops of 30-60 s, low contrast behind the presenter zone, brand color and a subtle motif. Provide a looping idle state plus a 3-5 s cue transition for walk-ons.

options.what: Continuous low-intensity motion inside an interface that signals life, status or presence without demanding action.
options.looks: Breathing glows, shimmering loaders, slowly shifting gradients, live indicators, subtle data ticks.
options.motion: Slow cycles (2-6 s), gentle opacity or scale oscillation, status pulses.
options.use: AI assistants, voice UIs, dashboards, lock screens, smart devices.
options.vs: UI micro-interactions respond to user input; ambient UI runs without input. A motion background has no functional meaning.
options.prompt: Add slow ambient cycles to the interface: a 3-5 s breathing glow on the active element (scale 1.00-1.03, opacity 70-100%), a shimmer on loading states, and a pulse on live indicators. Nothing faster than 2 s per cycle; all cycles loop seamlessly.
